lesson_title: The Great Depression and the New Deal
content_html:
The Wall Street Crash, 1929

On 24 October 1929 — “Black Thursday” — panic selling gripped the New York Stock Exchange. Share prices had been rising artificially throughout the 1920s, fuelled by buying on the margin. When confidence collapsed, investors raced to sell. By 29 October — “Black Tuesday” — the market had lost around 25 per cent of its value in days. Banks that had invested depositors’ money in shares now collapsed in turn, wiping out savings and triggering a chain of business failures.

Key Fact

The Wall Street Crash began on 24 October 1929 (“Black Thursday”) and worsened on 29 October (“Black Tuesday”). Within three years, around 13 million Americans were unemployed — roughly one in four workers.

Life During the Depression

By 1932, unemployment had reached approximately 25 per cent. Thousands of families lost their homes. The makeshift shanty towns that sprang up on the edges of cities became known as Hoovervilles — a bitter reference to the president many blamed for the crisis. Breadlines and soup kitchens became a feature of American cities. Farmers in the Midwest faced a double blow: banks repossessed farms while drought turned the Great Plains into a “Dust Bowl”, driving hundreds of thousands of “Okies” westward.

President Herbert Hoover was a firm believer in rugged individualism — the belief that government welfare would undermine Americans’ self-reliance. He refused to provide direct federal relief, fearing it would make people dependent on the state. His main measure, the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (RFC, 1932), gave loans to banks and large businesses, but the benefit was slow to reach ordinary Americans.

When around 20,000 First World War veterans marched on Washington in the summer of 1932 to demand early payment of a bonus promised for 1945, Hoover sent the army to clear their camps. Images of soldiers attacking veterans destroyed what remained of his popularity. In the November 1932 election, Roosevelt won 57 per cent of the popular vote.

Roosevelt and the New Deal

Franklin D. Roosevelt took office in March 1933 with the USA in the grip of a banking crisis. His inaugural address promised action: the government would treat the Depression as a national emergency equivalent to war. Roosevelt’s approach rested on three aims — Relief, Recovery and Reform — later called the “3 Rs”.

Key Fact

Roosevelt’s New Deal had three aims: Relief (immediate help for the unemployed and poor), Recovery (restarting the economy) and Reform (changing laws to prevent another crash). These goals drove the creation of the “alphabet agencies” during the Hundred Days of legislation in 1933.

The Hundred Days and Alphabet Agencies

Between March and June 1933 — the “Hundred Days” — Roosevelt pushed an extraordinary programme through Congress. He immediately declared a four-day bank holiday to stop panic withdrawals, then used radio “fireside chats” to reassure the public. Key agencies created in this period included:

The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC, 1933) put young unemployed men to work planting trees, building roads and maintaining national parks. Over its lifetime it employed approximately 3 million men. The Agricultural Adjustment Administration (AAA, 1933) paid farmers to reduce overproduction, raising crop prices. The National Recovery Administration (NRA, 1933) set codes for fair wages, prices and working conditions in industries, though the Supreme Court struck it down in 1935 as unconstitutional.

The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA, 1933) was one of the boldest measures — a federal body that built dams and hydroelectric power stations across seven states, bringing electricity to rural areas and creating thousands of construction jobs. The Works Progress Administration (WPA, 1935), created in the Second New Deal, employed millions on public works including roads, schools and hospitals, and also funded writers, artists and musicians.

The Second New Deal, 1935

By 1935 Roosevelt faced criticism from both the left and right. Senator Huey Long argued the New Deal had not done enough for the poor; business leaders complained of excessive government interference. Roosevelt responded with the Second New Deal. The Social Security Act (1935) established unemployment insurance and old-age pensions for the first time in American history. The Wagner Act (1935) guaranteed workers’ right to join trade unions and bargain collectively.

Opposition to the New Deal

Not everyone welcomed Roosevelt’s programme. Many Republicans and business leaders argued it amounted to socialism and damaged free enterprise. The Supreme Court declared several agencies unconstitutional. Critics like Huey Long called it too conservative. When Roosevelt tried to “pack” the Supreme Court with sympathetic justices in 1937, Congress blocked him — a significant political setback. Despite these tensions, the New Deal permanently changed expectations of what the federal government should provide for citizens.

lesson_title: Wartime economy and post-war affluence
content_html:
America Goes to War: The Wartime Economy

When Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, the USA entered the Second World War. The effect on the American economy was transformational. Factories that had made cars switched to producing tanks and aircraft. By 1944, the USA was manufacturing more war material than all the Axis powers combined. Unemployment — still around 14 per cent in 1940 — effectively disappeared as millions entered the armed forces and the defence industries absorbed the rest.

Key Fact

The Second World War ended the Great Depression more decisively than the New Deal had. By 1944, unemployment had fallen to below 2 per cent as 12 million Americans served in the armed forces and defence production boomed. GDP roughly doubled between 1939 and 1945.

Women and Minorities in the Wartime Workforce

With men away at war, women entered the workforce in unprecedented numbers. The image of Rosie the Riveter became a symbol of women’s wartime contribution. By 1944 around 19 million women held jobs, including in heavy industry. African American workers also moved north and west in large numbers — the so-called Great Migration accelerated — taking factory jobs in Detroit, Chicago and Los Angeles. Executive Order 8802 (1941), issued by President Roosevelt, banned racial discrimination in defence industries, though enforcement was uneven.

The GI Bill (1944), formally the Servicemen’s Readjustment Act, reshaped post-war America. It gave returning veterans access to low-cost mortgages, funding for college education, and small business loans. Around 8 million veterans used the education benefits, swelling university enrolments and creating a better-educated workforce. Cheap mortgages enabled millions of families to buy homes — fuelling the suburban expansion of the late 1940s and 1950s.

However, the GI Bill’s benefits were distributed unequally. African American veterans faced discrimination from banks that refused mortgages and from universities that denied admission. The bill inadvertently reinforced racial segregation in housing by making all-white suburbs accessible to white veterans while largely excluding Black Americans.

The Suburban Dream: Levittown and the 1950s Boom

Post-war prosperity transformed where and how Americans lived. Developer William Levitt mass-produced entire communities of affordable homes. Levittown (New York, from 1947) offered identical houses at prices veterans could afford with GI Bill mortgages. The car made commuting practical, and by the mid-1950s millions of families had left cities for the suburbs. Between 1950 and 1960, suburban populations grew by over 40 per cent.

Key Fact

The 1950s saw the rise of a consumer society: television ownership rose from around 9 per cent of homes in 1950 to nearly 90 per cent by 1960. Car ownership, refrigerators, washing machines and drive-in cinemas defined the decade. GDP grew strongly and real wages rose, giving many Americans a standard of living unprecedented in history.

Consumer Society and its Contradictions

The 1950s economy was powered by mass consumption. Advertisers used television to create demand for new products. Credit became widely available, and the concept of “keeping up with the Joneses” — matching neighbours’ material possessions — became a cultural force. The economy grew rapidly, and by the late 1950s the USA produced roughly half the world’s manufactured goods.

The interstate highway system, authorised by President Eisenhower in the Federal Aid Highway Act of 1956, was the largest public works project in American history. Over 41,000 miles of motorway were planned, linking every major city and transforming the movement of goods, people and military equipment. The highways deepened car dependency, gave a further boost to the automobile industry, and accelerated the shift of retail and employment from city centres to suburban sites. Shopping centres and drive-through restaurants became defining features of American culture during this decade.

Beneath the prosperity, deep inequalities persisted. In 1962, journalist and activist Michael Harrington published The Other America, arguing that between 40 and 50 million Americans — roughly a quarter of the population — lived in poverty invisible to the suburban mainstream. These were the rural poor of Appalachia, elderly Americans on fixed incomes, African Americans excluded from the post-war boom, and urban workers left behind by economic change.

The phrase “poverty amidst plenty” captured the paradox: the world’s wealthiest nation contained millions who could not afford adequate food, housing or healthcare. Harrington’s book influenced President Kennedy and contributed directly to President Johnson’s “War on Poverty” in the mid-1960s, which created Medicare, Medicaid and federal education funding through the Great Society programme.

lesson_title: Civil Rights, 1941-1955
content_html:
Black Americans and the War Effort

When the USA entered the Second World War in 1941, approximately 1 million African Americans served in the armed forces. Yet they did so in segregated units — the military operated under the same Jim Crow system of racial separation that governed life in the South. Black soldiers trained at segregated bases, were often assigned to labour rather than combat roles, and faced daily humiliations — some were refused service at lunch counters in towns near their bases while German prisoners of war were served without question.

African American civil rights leaders launched the Double V Campaign in 1942: Victory against fascism overseas and Victory against racism at home. The Pittsburgh Courier newspaper popularised the slogan. Though the campaign did not immediately change policy, it demonstrated that Black Americans' expectations had shifted — having fought for democracy abroad, they were no longer willing to accept second-class status at home.

Key Fact

Around 1 million Black Americans served in the Second World War in segregated units. The Double V Campaign (1942) demanded victory against fascism abroad AND discrimination at home. President Truman desegregated the armed forces by executive order in 1948 — a major early civil rights victory.

The Issue of Education: Brown v Board of Education, 1954

In 1896, the Supreme Court’s ruling in Plessy v Ferguson had established the doctrine of “separate but equal” — that segregated facilities were constitutional as long as they were equivalent in quality. In practice, Black schools received far less funding, had older buildings and fewer resources than white schools. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) mounted a legal challenge through the case of Oliver Brown, a parent in Topeka, Kansas.

On 17 May 1954, the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Brown v Board of Education of Topeka that racially segregated schools were inherently unequal and therefore unconstitutional. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that segregation generated “a feeling of inferiority” in Black children that harmed their educational development. The ruling was a landmark: it directly challenged the legal foundations of segregation. However, white resistance in the South was fierce — 101 Southern congressmen signed the “Southern Manifesto” in 1956 pledging to resist.

The challenge of desegregating schools became national news in September 1957 when nine Black students — the “Little Rock Nine” — attempted to enrol at Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas. Governor Orval Faubus called out the National Guard to block their entry. President Eisenhower, reluctant to intervene, eventually sent in 1,200 paratroopers of the 101st Airborne Division to escort the students safely past jeering crowds. Television broadcast the confrontation to millions of Americans and to the world — making the reality of Southern segregation impossible to ignore.

Emmett Till, 1955

In August 1955, Emmett Till, a 14-year-old Black teenager from Chicago, was visiting relatives in Money, Mississippi. He was abducted, brutally murdered and his body thrown into a river by two white men, Roy Bryant and J. W. Milam, following an alleged interaction with Bryant’s wife at a grocery store. The two men were acquitted by an all-white jury after deliberating for just 67 minutes. Till’s mother, Mamie Till-Mobley, insisted on an open-casket funeral so the world could see what had been done to her son. Photographs of Till’s body published in Jet magazine shocked the country and galvanised the civil rights movement.

Key Fact

Emmett Till was murdered in Mississippi in August 1955. His killers were acquitted by an all-white jury. His mother’s decision to hold an open-casket funeral and allow photographs of his body to be published brought the brutal reality of racial violence to national and international attention, energising the civil rights movement.

The Montgomery Bus Boycott, 1955–1956

On 1 December 1955, Rosa Parks, a Black seamstress and NAACP activist in Montgomery, Alabama, refused to give up her seat to a white passenger on a city bus — as required by local segregation ordinances. She was arrested. Local civil rights leaders, including the Reverend Martin Luther King Jr., organised a boycott of the bus system. For 381 days, the vast majority of Black Montgomerians walked, cycled or carpooled rather than use the buses. The city’s bus company, which relied on Black passengers for around 70 per cent of its revenue, suffered serious financial losses.

In November 1956, the Supreme Court ruled in Browder v Gayle that bus segregation in Montgomery was unconstitutional. The boycott ended in December 1956 with the buses desegregated. The significance went far beyond Montgomery: it demonstrated that organised, disciplined, non-violent mass protest could succeed; it launched Martin Luther King Jr. as a national figure; and it provided a model of protest that would be replicated across the South. The Montgomery Improvement Association, which led the boycott, evolved into the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC).

lesson_title: Civil Rights, 1955-1970: King, Malcolm X and legislation
content_html:
Birmingham, Alabama, 1963

By 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) chose Birmingham, Alabama — one of the most segregated cities in the South — as the location for a major campaign. The city’s Public Safety Commissioner, Bull Connor, could be relied upon to react with violence, generating the televised images the movement needed to build national pressure. When protesters — including schoolchildren — were met with fire hoses and police dogs, footage broadcast across the country and around the world created international outrage. President Kennedy was moved to call for federal civil rights legislation.

Key Fact

The Birmingham campaign of 1963 used Bull Connor’s violent response to peaceful protest — including the use of fire hoses and dogs against children — to generate televised images that shocked the nation. It directly led President Kennedy to propose what became the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

The March on Washington, August 1963

On 28 August 1963, approximately 250,000 people — Black and white — gathered in Washington D.C. for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. It was the largest civil rights demonstration in American history to that point. At the Lincoln Memorial, Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his address in which he described his vision of an America where people would not be judged by the colour of their skin but by the content of their character. The march demonstrated the breadth of support for civil rights and put enormous political pressure on Congress to pass legislation.

President Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas on 22 November 1963. His successor, Lyndon B. Johnson, used Kennedy’s legacy and his own considerable congressional skill to push the Civil Rights Act (1964) through Congress. The Act outlawed discrimination in employment and public places, ending the legal basis for racial segregation in hotels, restaurants and other public facilities.

The Selma to Montgomery marches of March 1965 were the final catalyst for voting rights legislation. When marchers crossing the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma were beaten by state troopers on “Bloody Sunday” (7 March 1965), the televised scenes of violence shocked President Johnson into action. The Voting Rights Act (1965) banned literacy tests and other devices used to stop Black Americans from registering to vote. Within three years, Black voter registration in the South rose dramatically.

Malcolm X and Black Nationalism

While King advocated non-violent integration, Malcolm X offered a sharply different approach. Born Malcolm Little, he had converted to the Nation of Islam while in prison. The Nation, led by Elijah Muhammad, preached that white society was fundamentally racist and that Black Americans should build separate institutions rather than seek integration. Malcolm X was a brilliant speaker who rejected what he called the “turn the other cheek” strategy, arguing that Black Americans had the right to defend themselves by any means necessary.

In 1964, Malcolm X broke with the Nation of Islam, made a pilgrimage to Mecca, and developed a more inclusive worldview — acknowledging that not all white people were enemies. He was assassinated in February 1965. His life inspired the later Black Power movement and his Autobiography, published posthumously, became deeply influential.

Key Fact

King advocated non-violent direct action aimed at integrating Black Americans into mainstream society. Malcolm X — at least until 1964 — advocated Black nationalism and self-defence. Both challenged white supremacy but through fundamentally different strategies. Historians debate which approach was more effective in achieving change.

Black Power, 1966–1970

After 1965, frustration grew within the civil rights movement, particularly in Northern cities where legal segregation did not exist but economic inequality and police brutality persisted. A wave of urban rebellions — in Watts, Los Angeles (1965), Detroit and Newark (1967) — reflected this anger. In 1966, SNCC leader Stokely Carmichael popularised the slogan “Black Power,” calling for Black economic and political self-determination. The Black Panther Party, founded in Oakland in 1966 by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale, combined armed self-defence patrols with community programmes providing free breakfasts for children.

On 4 April 1968, Martin Luther King Jr. was shot and killed in Memphis, Tennessee, where he had gone to support striking sanitation workers — most of whom were Black. His assassination provoked riots in more than 100 American cities. The Fair Housing Act (1968), passed in the days following his death, banned racial discrimination in the sale or rental of housing — completing the major legislative achievements of the civil rights era. King’s death marked both the loss of the movement’s most powerful unifying voice and the transition into a more fragmented post-civil-rights era.

lesson_title: Political change, 1960-2000: from Kennedy to Clinton
content_html:
Kennedy and the New Frontier, 1961–1963

John F. Kennedy was inaugurated as the 35th President of the United States on 20 January 1961, the youngest man ever elected to the office. His domestic programme — the New Frontier — was ambitious: expanding federal aid to education, introducing Medicare to provide healthcare for the elderly, protecting civil rights and tackling poverty. However, Kennedy faced a conservative Congress that blocked much of his domestic agenda. He had more success in foreign policy, particularly in managing the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) and launching the Space Race with the Apollo programme.

Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, on 22 November 1963. His vice president, Lyndon B. Johnson, used Kennedy’s memory and his own political skill to pass landmark legislation that Kennedy had been unable to get through Congress, including the Civil Rights Act (1964) and his “Great Society” programme of welfare expansion.

Key Fact

Kennedy’s New Frontier aimed to tackle poverty, extend civil rights, expand education and create Medicare. Much was blocked by Congress during his lifetime. After his assassination (22 November 1963), Johnson’s Great Society actually delivered many of these goals, including Medicare (1965) and the Civil Rights Act (1964).

Nixon and Watergate, 1972–1974

Richard Nixon won the 1968 and 1972 presidential elections by large margins. He achieved significant foreign policy successes — opening diplomatic relations with China in 1972 and negotiating the SALT I arms limitation treaty with the USSR. However, his presidency was destroyed by the Watergate scandal. On 17 June 1972, operatives working for Nixon’s re-election campaign broke into the Democratic Party headquarters at the Watergate Hotel in Washington D.C. to plant listening devices. Nixon was not directly involved in ordering the break-in, but he participated in covering up the White House connection.

Investigative journalists from the Washington Post and Congressional investigations gradually exposed the cover-up. White House tape recordings proved Nixon’s involvement. When the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in United States v Nixon (1974) that he must hand over the tapes, impeachment became inevitable. Nixon resigned on 9 August 1974 — the only US president to have resigned from office. Vice President Gerald Ford assumed the presidency and controversially pardoned Nixon.

Watergate had profound effects on American political life. Public trust in government collapsed: opinion polls from the late 1970s showed record levels of cynicism about political institutions. Congress passed the War Powers Act (1973) and campaign finance reform legislation to limit executive power. The suffix “-gate” entered the language to describe political scandals.

The Reagan Years, 1981–1989

Ronald Reagan won the 1980 election in a landslide, capitalising on economic stagflation and the Iran hostage crisis under President Carter. Reagan’s domestic economic programme — nicknamed Reaganomics — combined large tax cuts (particularly for high earners), deregulation of industries, reduced federal spending on social programmes and tight monetary policy. Supporters argued this “trickle-down” approach unleashed economic growth; critics argued it increased inequality and cut services for the poor.

Key Fact

Reaganomics combined tax cuts, deregulation, reduced social spending and tight monetary control. By the mid-1980s inflation had fallen sharply and economic growth resumed. However, income inequality grew and the federal deficit increased substantially as tax cuts outpaced spending reductions. Reagan also tripled the national debt during his presidency.

George H. W. Bush and Bill Clinton

Reagan’s vice president, George H. W. Bush, won the 1988 election but lost to Bill Clinton in 1992 largely because of a recession. Clinton’s campaign emphasised economic issues with the phrase “It’s the economy, stupid.” Clinton presided over a prolonged economic expansion in the 1990s, aided by the technology boom. He pursued centrist “Third Way” politics — accepting elements of both liberal and conservative approaches — and oversaw welfare reform (1996) that reduced the federal welfare rolls.

Despite his economic record, Clinton’s second term was dominated by scandal. He was impeached by the House of Representatives in December 1998 on charges of perjury and obstruction of justice related to his relationship with a White House intern. The Senate acquitted him in February 1999, and he remained in office. The episode was seen by many as a politically motivated attack by Republican opponents; others saw it as a serious matter of presidential integrity. Clinton left office in January 2001 with high approval ratings.

lesson_title: Social change, 1950-2000
content_html:
Rock ‘n’ Roll and the Teenagers of the 1950s

In the early 1950s a new musical form emerged from the fusion of African American rhythm and blues with country music. When Elvis Presley recorded “That’s All Right” in Memphis in 1954, rock and roll had its first mainstream star. Presley’s swivelling hips and uninhibited stage style scandalised parents and conservative commentators — he was initially shown only from the waist up on television. Rock and roll sold to white teenagers music rooted in Black culture, contributing to a gradual cultural integration, though the original Black artists — Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino — were often paid less and reached smaller audiences than their white counterparts.

Key Fact

Rock and roll emerged in the mid-1950s, with Elvis Presley its most visible white star. It challenged racial barriers (fusing Black and white musical traditions) and generational norms (celebrating youth rebellion). Television — which reached nearly 90 per cent of American homes by 1960 — gave rock and roll national reach and created the first true teenage mass market.

The 1960s Counterculture

By the mid-1960s, a broader counterculture had emerged among young Americans. The “hippie” movement rejected materialism, the Vietnam War, and conventional social norms. Young people gathered at events like the Woodstock music festival in August 1969 — attended by approximately 400,000 people — as a celebration of peace, music and alternative values. Student protests against the Vietnam War spread to campuses across the country; at Kent State University, Ohio, in May 1970, National Guardsmen shot and killed four students during a protest, shocking the nation.

In the early hours of 28 June 1969, police raided the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in New York City’s Greenwich Village. Instead of submitting to arrest as had been customary, the patrons — many of them transgender women, drag queens and homeless youth — fought back. The Stonewall uprising lasted several days and galvanised the gay rights movement. The first Pride march in New York took place in June 1970. By the 1980s and 1990s, gay rights organisations had become a significant force in American politics, though the AIDS crisis of the 1980s devastated gay communities and highlighted ongoing discrimination in healthcare and government responses.

Second-Wave Feminism

The women’s movement underwent a revival in the 1960s and 1970s. Betty Friedan’s influential 1963 book The Feminine Mystique argued that middle-class American women were trapped in a domestic role that left them unfulfilled. In 1966, Friedan co-founded the National Organization for Women (NOW) to campaign for equal rights. Second-wave feminism made significant legal gains: the Equal Pay Act (1963) mandated equal pay for the same work; the Civil Rights Act (1964) banned sex discrimination in employment; Roe v Wade (1973) established the constitutional right to abortion.

Key Fact

Key legal milestones for women’s rights: Equal Pay Act (1963), sex discrimination banned under the Civil Rights Act (1964), and Roe v Wade (1973) legalising abortion nationwide. However, the proposed Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), passed by Congress in 1972, was never ratified by the required number of states, blocked in part by a conservative backlash organised by activist Phyllis Schlafly.

Media, Entertainment and Cultural Change, 1950–2000

Television transformed American culture from the 1950s onwards. By the 1980s, MTV (launched August 1981) was reshaping the music industry by creating a visual dimension to popular music and making image as important as sound. Hip hop, emerging from New York’s Black and Latino communities in the late 1970s, grew from local party music into one of the world’s most commercially successful genres by the 1990s, carrying messages about urban poverty, police brutality and racial identity to mainstream audiences.

The 1990s brought the internet into American homes. The World Wide Web became publicly accessible in the early 1990s, and by 2000 around 50 per cent of US households had internet access. Online retail, email and digital media began to transform commerce, communication and entertainment — setting the stage for the social media revolution of the twenty-first century. The 1990s technology boom also drove the economic expansion that characterised the Clinton years, though the “dotcom bubble” burst in 2000 wiping out trillions of dollars of stock market value.

lesson_title: Cold War rivalry, 1945-1973
content_html:
Origins of the Cold War: Truman Doctrine and Containment

By 1947, the wartime alliance between the USA and Soviet Union had broken down. The USA was alarmed by Soviet pressure on Turkey, Communist insurgencies in Greece, and the Soviet installation of Communist governments across Eastern Europe. President Harry Truman responded in March 1947 with what became known as the Truman Doctrine: the USA would support free peoples resisting subjugation by armed minorities or outside pressures. Congress voted 400 million dollars in military and economic aid to Greece and Turkey. The accompanying Marshall Plan (1948) provided around 13 billion dollars to rebuild Western European economies — partly to make communism less attractive by alleviating post-war poverty.

Key Fact

The Truman Doctrine (March 1947) committed the USA to containing communism by supporting threatened nations — the policy became known as containment. The Marshall Plan (1948) provided approximately 13 billion dollars for European reconstruction. Both policies aimed to prevent Western Europe from falling to communism through poverty or subversion.

The Berlin Crisis and Airlift, 1948–1949

Berlin, the former German capital, lay deep inside the Soviet occupation zone. In June 1948, the Soviet Union blockaded all land and water routes into West Berlin, hoping to force the Western Allies to abandon the city or accept Soviet terms for its future. President Truman’s response was the Berlin Airlift: for 323 days, American and British aircraft flew in all supplies required by the city’s 2 million inhabitants — at its peak delivering nearly 13,000 tonnes of goods per day. In May 1949, the Soviets ended the blockade. The airlift was a propaganda victory for the West, demonstrating American resolve and technological capacity.

In June 1950, Communist North Korea invaded South Korea. The United Nations (dominated by the USA after the Soviet Union was temporarily boycotting the Security Council) intervened under US command. The Korean War was a direct application of containment: UN forces, primarily American, fought to prevent the communist North from conquering the South. When China entered the war in late 1950, the conflict widened. An armistice was signed in July 1953, restoring roughly the pre-war border. Around 36,500 American soldiers died in the conflict.

The Nuclear Arms Race and NATO

Alongside the diplomatic and military confrontations, the USA and Soviet Union engaged in a relentless nuclear arms race. The USA had used atomic bombs against Japan in August 1945; the Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in September 1949, far sooner than American scientists had predicted. By the early 1950s, both sides were developing the far more powerful hydrogen bomb. The USA tested its first hydrogen bomb in November 1952; the Soviet Union followed in August 1953. The prospect of mutually assured destruction — that any nuclear exchange would destroy both sides — became the grim logic underpinning Cold War stability. To formalise Western defence commitments, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) was founded in April 1949, committing its members to treat an attack on any one of them as an attack on all. The Soviet Union responded by forming the Warsaw Pact in 1955. These rival alliances divided Europe into two armed camps for four decades.

The Cuban Missile Crisis, 1962

In October 1962, American U-2 spy planes photographed Soviet nuclear missile installations under construction in Cuba, just 90 miles from the Florida coast. President Kennedy was briefed on 16 October. The discovery triggered the most dangerous episode of the Cold War — a 13-day standoff in which the world came perilously close to nuclear war. Kennedy established a naval blockade of Cuba, demanding the removal of the missiles. Soviet ships carrying further military equipment were on course for Cuba.

Key Fact

The Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) lasted 13 days. It was resolved when Soviet leader Khrushchev agreed to remove missiles from Cuba in exchange for a US pledge not to invade Cuba and (secretly) the removal of US missiles from Turkey. The crisis led directly to the establishment of a direct hotline between Washington and Moscow to prevent future miscommunication.

US Involvement in Vietnam

Vietnam had been divided since 1954 — Communist North Vietnam under Ho Chi Minh and a US-backed South. American military advisers were present from the late 1950s. The war escalated dramatically after the Gulf of Tonkin incident in August 1964, when Congress passed a resolution giving President Johnson broad authority to escalate US military involvement. By 1968, over 500,000 American troops were deployed in Vietnam.

Television brought the Vietnam War into American living rooms in unprecedented detail. The Tet Offensive (January 1968), in which Communist forces launched coordinated attacks on South Vietnamese cities, shattered the US government’s claims that the war was being won. Anti-war protests grew on university campuses and in cities. The revelation that American forces had massacred civilians at My Lai village in March 1968 (revealed publicly in 1969) deepened public disillusionment. President Nixon began withdrawing troops from 1969 under his “Vietnamisation” strategy, and the last US combat troops left in 1973. South Vietnam fell to the North in April 1975. Approximately 58,000 Americans died in the conflict.

lesson_title: Détente and the end of the Cold War, 1970-1991
content_html:
What was Détente?

By the early 1970s, both the USA and Soviet Union had accumulated enough nuclear weapons to destroy each other many times over. The Vietnam War had damaged American confidence and drained resources. Both superpowers had incentives to reduce tensions and limit the escalating cost of the arms race. The result was détente — a French word meaning “relaxation.” It marked a pragmatic recognition by both sides that confrontation carried unacceptable risks.

Key Fact

SALT I (1972) was the first major nuclear arms limitation agreement, signed by President Nixon and Soviet leader Brezhnev. It froze the number of intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) and submarine-launched missiles each side could hold. SALT II (1979) set further limits on nuclear warheads but was never ratified by the US Senate after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979.

Nixon Opens Relations with China, 1972

One of the most unexpected diplomatic moves of the Cold War was Nixon’s decision to open relations with the People’s Republic of China. Since the Communist victory in China’s civil war in 1949, the USA had refused to recognise the Beijing government, instead treating Taiwan as the legitimate Chinese government. Nixon, a lifelong anti-communist, recognised that China and the Soviet Union had their own territorial disputes and that playing the two powers against each other could benefit American diplomacy — a strategy known as triangular diplomacy.

In February 1972, Nixon visited China — the first sitting US president to do so — meeting Communist leader Mao Zedong. The visit, nicknamed “ping-pong diplomacy” because it had been preceded by a cultural exchange between the two countries’ table tennis teams, opened the door to normalisation of relations, completed under President Carter in 1979.

The Limits of Détente

Détente had its limits. The Helsinki Accords (1975), signed by 35 nations including the USA and USSR, recognised post-war European borders and contained human rights commitments — which Soviet dissidents later used to hold their government to account. However, détente did not stop superpower competition in the developing world. The USA and USSR backed rival factions in conflicts in Angola, Ethiopia and elsewhere throughout the 1970s. American confidence was further damaged by President Carter’s perceived weakness during the 1979 Tehran hostage crisis. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 was the decisive blow: Carter withdrew the USA from the 1980 Moscow Olympics and the US Senate refused to ratify SALT II, effectively ending the détente era. By the time Ronald Reagan took office in January 1981, the mood in Washington had decisively shifted back towards confrontation with the Soviet Union.

Ronald Reagan entered office in 1981 determined to reverse détente and reassert American strength. In a 1983 speech he described the Soviet Union as an Evil Empire, signalling a return to confrontational rhetoric. Reagan dramatically increased US defence spending and proposed the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI — nicknamed “Star Wars”), a space-based missile defence system. Historians debate whether SDI was intended to be built or was a negotiating bluff designed to force the Soviets into an unwinnable spending race.

The USA also supported anti-communist forces around the world under the “Reagan Doctrine,” providing arms to groups fighting Soviet-backed governments in Afghanistan, Nicaragua and Angola. The Soviet intervention in Afghanistan (1979–1989) became a costly quagmire for the USSR, often compared to America’s Vietnam experience.

Gorbachev and the End of the Cold War

When Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in 1985, the USSR faced severe economic stagnation. Gorbachev introduced two transformative reform programmes: perestroika (economic restructuring) and glasnost (openness and greater freedom of expression). He also sought to reduce the Cold War arms burden by negotiating with Reagan. The INF Treaty (1987) eliminated an entire class of nuclear weapons — intermediate-range missiles — for the first time.

Key Fact

Gorbachev’s reforms of the mid-1980s — perestroika (economic restructuring) and glasnost (openness) — were intended to save the Soviet system, but they fatally undermined it by unleashing demands for greater freedoms. By 1989, Soviet satellite states in Eastern Europe were holding free elections; the Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989. The USSR itself was dissolved on 25 December 1991.

On the night of 9 November 1989, the East German government announced that citizens could cross freely through the Berlin Wall, which had divided the city since 1961. Crowds gathered and began physically demolishing it. The images broadcast worldwide symbolised the collapse of Communist authority in Eastern Europe. Within months, free elections were held across the former Soviet bloc. Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990. The dissolution of the Soviet Union on 25 December 1991 formally ended the Cold War — a conflict that had structured world affairs for over four decades.

lesson_title: US involvement in Iran, Iraq and the Gulf War
content_html:
The Iranian Revolution and Hostage Crisis, 1979

Since 1953, the USA had strongly supported the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose regime received American military and financial backing in exchange for oil supplies and a strategic anti-communist alliance. Many Iranians resented what they saw as American interference in their country’s affairs. In January 1979, mass protests and a revolution drove the Shah into exile. The revolution was led by Ayatollah Khomeini, a Shia cleric who established an Islamic Republic.

On 4 November 1979, Iranian students stormed the US Embassy in Tehran and took 52 American diplomats hostage. The Tehran hostage crisis lasted 444 days and proved deeply damaging to President Carter’s presidency. A military rescue attempt, Operation Eagle Claw (April 1980), failed catastrophically when helicopters crashed in the Iranian desert. The hostages were only released on 20 January 1981 — the day Ronald Reagan was inaugurated as president.

Key Fact

The Iranian Revolution (January 1979) replaced the US-backed Shah with Ayatollah Khomeini’s Islamic Republic. The Tehran hostage crisis began on 4 November 1979 when 52 US diplomats were seized; it lasted 444 days and ended on 20 January 1981 — the day Reagan took office. It severely damaged Carter’s re-election prospects.

The Iran-Iraq War and US Policy, 1980–1988

In September 1980, Iraq’s president, Saddam Hussein, ordered an invasion of revolutionary Iran, hoping to exploit the chaos of the revolution and seize the oil-rich Khuzestan region. The USA, alarmed by the Islamic Republic’s hostility, provided significant support to Iraq during the war — including intelligence, agricultural credits, and dual-use technology that could be used for weapons development. The war lasted eight years and cost approximately 500,000 to 1 million lives before ending inconclusively in August 1988.

The United States’ support for Iraq during this war was later cited as a damaging inconsistency in American foreign policy. By backing Saddam Hussein’s regime, the USA helped build up the very military machine that would threaten regional stability less than two years after the war ended. The USS Stark incident of May 1987 — in which an Iraqi aircraft fired missiles at an American frigate, killing 37 sailors — was treated with restraint by the Reagan administration, illustrating how strongly the USA prioritised containing Iran over confronting Iraq. This context made it deeply embarrassing when Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in 1990, forcing the USA to mobilise against a regime it had recently been supporting.

Having been armed and supported by the USA during the Iran-Iraq War, Saddam Hussein turned aggressively westward. On 2 August 1990, Iraqi forces invaded neighbouring Kuwait, a small but oil-rich emirate. Saddam claimed Kuwait as historically part of Iraq and resented Kuwait’s alleged overproduction of oil that was depressing prices. The international community, including the Arab League, condemned the invasion. The United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 678 in November 1990, authorising the use of force to expel Iraq from Kuwait if it had not withdrawn by 15 January 1991.

Operation Desert Storm, 1991

Under President George H. W. Bush, the USA assembled a coalition of 35 nations — including Arab states such as Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Syria — to liberate Kuwait. This diplomatic achievement was seen as one of Bush’s greatest successes. Operation Desert Storm began on 17 January 1991 with an intensive air campaign that degraded Iraqi military infrastructure. The ground offensive began on 24 February 1991 and lasted just 100 hours before Kuwait was liberated. Iraqi forces suffered heavy casualties; Kuwait was freed with relatively low coalition losses.

Key Fact

Operation Desert Storm (January–February 1991) combined an intensive six-week air campaign with a ground war that lasted just 100 hours. The coalition of 35 nations, assembled by President Bush, liberated Kuwait. Bush chose not to advance to Baghdad and remove Saddam Hussein, believing it would destabilise the region and break up the coalition.

Bush’s decision to end the war at Kuwait’s liberation rather than marching on Baghdad was controversial. Supporters argued it was consistent with the UN mandate (which authorised expelling Iraq from Kuwait, not regime change) and with preserving the Arab coalition. Critics argued it left Saddam Hussein in power and required the USA to maintain a large military presence in Saudi Arabia — which became a grievance cited by Osama bin Laden and contributed to later conflict. The unresolved question of Iraq would dominate US foreign policy for the following decade.

lesson_title: Themes across the period: continuity and change
content_html:
Thinking Thematically: Change and Continuity Across Seven Decades

Studying the USA from 1929 to 2000 means tracking change and continuity across four interconnected areas: the economy, politics, society and foreign policy. Examiners reward students who can synthesise across the period — spotting patterns, turning points, and areas where things stayed the same despite surface changes. This lesson helps you build those connections.

The Economy: From Depression to Superpower

The American economy in 1929 was a capitalist market economy with minimal federal government intervention. The Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression shattered confidence in laissez-faire economics — the belief that markets regulate themselves best without government interference. Roosevelt’s New Deal permanently expanded the federal government’s economic role. The Second World War delivered the full employment the New Deal had not: by 1944 unemployment was below 2 per cent. Post-war prosperity (1945–1970) produced the world’s largest consumer economy.

Key Fact

Economic continuity: the USA remained a capitalist economy throughout 1929–2000. Economic change: the federal government’s role expanded dramatically — from Hoover’s laissez-faire to Roosevelt’s New Deal (1933), Johnson’s Great Society (1965), and Reagan’s rollback of welfare spending (1981). Reagan shifted the dial back towards free markets, but the New Deal’s Social Security Act remained in place.

Politics: From Small Government to Big Government and Back

American politics between 1929 and 2000 was shaped by a fundamental debate about the role of federal government. Hoover represented the old tradition of minimal intervention. Roosevelt broke that tradition decisively with the New Deal. After the Second World War, Truman, Kennedy and Johnson expanded federal responsibility further — civil rights legislation, Medicare, Medicaid, federal education funding. Then Reagan led a conservative revolution from 1981 that sought to reverse this trend, cutting taxes and deregulating industries. Clinton’s “Third Way” in the 1990s accepted the broad framework of both: market economics plus a safety net.

Political scandal was a recurring feature of the period. Harding’s Teapot Dome scandal (1924) predated the period, but Watergate (1972–74) resulted in the first presidential resignation. The Iran-Contra affair (1986–87) — in which Reagan administration officials secretly sold arms to Iran and used the proceeds to fund Nicaraguan rebels — damaged Reagan’s second term. Clinton’s impeachment (1998) showed that personal conduct had become a political weapon. Each scandal reinforced public cynicism about government, but the constitutional system survived each test.

Society: How Much Did America Change?

Social change was profound but uneven. African Americans moved from the legal basis of the Jim Crow system (which dated from the post-Civil War era) to federal civil rights protection by 1968 — a transformation in law. But economic and social equality remained incomplete: unemployment rates among Black Americans remained roughly double white rates throughout the period. Women gained legal equality in employment and reproductive rights, yet faced a glass ceiling in corporate and political leadership. The uneven pace of change is itself an argument you can deploy in extended responses.

Key Fact

Between 1929 and 2000, significant social changes included: civil rights legislation (1964–68); women’s legal equality (Equal Pay Act 1963, Roe v Wade 1973); media transformation (radio to TV to internet); and the rise of a mass consumer middle class. Persistent inequalities included: racial economic gaps; gender pay gap; poverty (Harrington counted 40–50 million poor in 1962); and the gap between suburban prosperity and urban poverty.

Foreign Policy: From Isolation to Superpower

In 1929 the USA was not formally isolationist but it avoided European entanglements. Pearl Harbor (December 1941) ended that era permanently. After 1945, the USA was irreversibly a global superpower: founding member of the UN and NATO, the world’s largest economy, possessor of nuclear weapons. The Cold War structured US foreign policy from 1947 until 1991 — every military intervention (Korea, Vietnam, Gulf War) was framed through the lens of containing communism or managing the post-Cold War order. The end of the Cold War in 1991 left the USA as the world’s sole superpower, but the Gulf War demonstrated that the threats requiring military response had changed.

Major turning points include: 1933 (New Deal — federal government permanently expanded); 1941 (Pearl Harbor — isolationism ended); 1954 (Brown v Board — legal segregation challenged); 1963-68 (civil rights legislation — Jim Crow ended legally); 1974 (Nixon resignation — constitutional checks on presidential power tested); 1980-81 (Reagan revolution — ideological shift to conservatism); 1991 (Gulf War + USSR dissolved — Cold War ended). When writing extended essays, use these as pegs to organise your argument about how much change occurred and what caused it.

lesson_title: Exam technique: 16-mark period essays
content_html:
Understanding the 16-Mark Period Essay

The 16-mark extended essay is the highest-tariff question in the Period Study component. It tests your ability to construct a substantiated judgement. This means more than writing a lot — examiners want you to argue a position, support it with precise evidence, acknowledge the strongest counter-arguments, and then reach a clear conclusion that answers the question directly. A student who writes three pages of description without arguing a position will cap at around the middle band.

Key Fact

A top-band 16-mark essay has three non-negotiable features: (1) An argument — your thesis stated upfront, not after several paragraphs of description. (2) Precise evidence — named dates, people, acts, statistics specific to this period. (3) A substantiated overall judgement — a conclusion that directly answers the question by weighing the evidence, not merely summarising what you’ve written.

Dissecting a Typical Question

Period essay questions follow a predictable pattern. Examples include:

  • “How far was the New Deal the main reason for America’s economic recovery?”
  • “The civil rights movement achieved more through legal action than through direct protest.’ How far do you agree?”
  • “How significant was the role of the president in bringing about change in the USA between 1929 and 2000?”

All three questions share a structure: they name one factor (or claim) and ask “how far” or “how significant.” Your job is to weigh that factor against others and reach a verdict. A common error is to agree entirely with the question’s claim: this removes the complexity the examiner is testing. Even if the named factor is genuinely the most important, you must engage with the others and explain why they are less significant.

A reliable paragraph structure is PEEL: Point (state your argument in one sentence), Evidence (specific names, dates, acts, statistics), Explanation (how the evidence supports your argument), Link (connect back to the question). For a 16-mark essay you need at least two paragraphs arguing one side, one paragraph engaging with the counter-argument, and a conclusion. Aim for three to four focused paragraphs plus introduction and conclusion in approximately 45 minutes.

Timing tip: do not spend more than 5 minutes planning, but do plan. A one-minute bullet-point plan stops you from writing yourself into a narrative summary instead of an argument. Write your thesis — your answer to the question — in the first sentence of your introduction, not the last sentence of your conclusion.

What Examiners Mean by ‘Factor Weighting’

Factor weighting means you do not just describe two causes — you argue which was more important and why. Comparison language is your friend: “Although the New Deal provided immediate relief, it was ultimately the Second World War that achieved genuine full employment because…” The phrase “because” is doing the analytical work. Avoid: “On the one hand… On the other hand…” structures that describe both sides without ever weighing them.

Key Fact

Useful analytical phrases for the 16-mark essay: “The most significant factor was… because…”; “Although X contributed to change, Y was ultimately more important because…”; “The evidence suggests that X mattered more than Y in the long term because…”; “While X achieved [specific outcome], it did not address [specific limit], which is why Y was also crucial.”

Structuring a Response: Worked Example

Question: “How far was the New Deal the main reason for economic change in the USA between 1933 and 1945?”

Thesis (first sentence): “The New Deal was a significant but ultimately incomplete cause of economic change — the Second World War proved more transformative by eliminating unemployment and doubling GDP.”

Para 1 — New Deal’s importance: Alphabet agencies (CCC employed 3 million; TVA brought electricity to rural areas; WPA employed millions on public works); Social Security Act created safety net; reduced unemployment from 25% to around 15% by 1937. But: 1937 recession when Roosevelt cut spending proved the recovery was fragile.

Para 2 — The decisive role of the war: By 1944 unemployment below 2%. GDP roughly doubled 1939–1945. Defence production absorbed remaining unemployed. The New Deal provided relief and reform; the war delivered genuine full employment and industrial transformation. This supports the argument that the war was the main cause of economic change.

Counter-argument / concession: Without the New Deal’s banking reforms and Social Security Act, the US economic and social infrastructure might have been too damaged to sustain wartime production. The New Deal created the conditions for recovery; the war delivered it.

Conclusion: “Overall, although the New Deal was crucial in preventing total economic collapse and creating the conditions for recovery, it was the Second World War that brought decisive economic change. The New Deal mattered more for relief and structural reform; the war mattered more for economic recovery itself.”

lesson_title: Weimar Germany, 1919-1933: a survey
content_html:
Germany After the First World War

When Germany signed the armistice in November 1918, the Kaiser abdicated and a new democratic republic was proclaimed. The new government inherited enormous problems: a nation exhausted by four years of war, millions of dead and wounded, and a people who had been told the war was going well right up until the defeat. Many Germans felt humiliated and confused by the sudden collapse.

The Weimar Republic took its name from the city where its constitution was written in 1919. Germany’s new constitution created one of the most democratic systems in the world at that time, with universal suffrage — votes for all adults — and proportional representation in the Reichstag. It also included Article 48, which allowed the president to govern by emergency decree without consulting parliament, a clause that would later be fatally misused.

Key Fact

The Treaty of Versailles (1919) forced Germany to accept war guilt (Article 231), pay reparations set at £132 billion in 1921, lose 13% of its territory and 10% of its population, and reduce its army to 100,000 men.

The Treaty of Versailles and Its Impact

Signed in June 1919, the Treaty of Versailles caused immediate outrage in Germany. The ‘war guilt’ clause (Article 231) forced Germany to accept sole responsibility for the war. Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine to France, the Polish Corridor was created dividing East Prussia from the rest of Germany, and the Rhineland was demilitarised and occupied by Allied troops. German colonies were handed to the victorious powers as League of Nations mandates. Many Germans called the settlement a ‘Diktat’ — a dictated peace — imposed without any German input in negotiations.

Politicians who signed the armistice and accepted Versailles were labelled ‘November criminals’ by nationalist critics. This stab-in-the-back myth — the idea that Germany had been betrayed from within, not defeated in battle — became a powerful propaganda weapon against the Weimar Republic throughout its existence.

Early Crises: Left and Right Challenges

The Weimar Republic faced violent challenges from both left and right almost immediately. In January 1919, the Spartacist Rising attempted to establish a Soviet-style republic in Berlin. The government used the Freikorps — irregular right-wing soldiers — to crush the revolt; its leaders, Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, were murdered. This decision embedded deep hostility between the Social Democrats and the German communist left.

In March 1920, the Kapp Putsch brought a challenge from the right. Wolfgang Kapp led Freikorps troops to seize Berlin, declaring the Weimar government overthrown. The army refused to act against the rebels. The putsch failed only because Berlin workers called a general strike, paralysing the capital. The republic had been saved by the workers, not the military — revealing how fragile its institutional loyalties were.

In November 1923, at the height of the economic crisis, Adolf Hitler led the Nazi Party in an attempted coup in Munich. He believed the moment of maximum chaos was the right time to seize power. The putsch collapsed when police opened fire on the marchers; sixteen Nazis and four police officers were killed. Hitler was arrested and sentenced to five years in prison, though he served only nine months. During his imprisonment he wrote Mein Kampf. The failure of the putsch convinced Hitler that power had to be won through elections, not armed uprising.

Hyperinflation 1923

Germany’s economy was already under severe strain from reparations payments when, in January 1923, France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr industrial region, claiming Germany had defaulted on timber deliveries. The Weimar government ordered passive resistance — workers refused to cooperate with the occupiers but needed to be paid. The government printed money to fund the campaign, triggering catastrophic hyperinflation.

By November 1923 a loaf of bread cost billions of marks. Savings accumulated over decades were wiped out almost overnight. Those on fixed incomes — pensioners, civil servants — were ruined. People carried money in wheelbarrows to buy basic goods. The psychological impact of hyperinflation on the German middle class was lasting: it generated a deep distrust of the democratic republic and its ability to manage the economy.

Key Fact

Stresemann’s recovery in 1923–24 rested on three pillars: ending passive resistance in the Ruhr, replacing the worthless mark with a new currency (the Rentenmark), and negotiating the Dawes Plan (1924) to reschedule reparations with US loans.

Stresemann and the Golden Twenties

Gustav Stresemann served as chancellor briefly in 1923 and then as foreign minister until his death in October 1929. He ended passive resistance in the Ruhr, stabilised the currency, and set Germany on a path of recovery. The Dawes Plan of 1924 brought American loans and restructured reparations, allowing industry to recover. US investment poured into Germany throughout the mid-1920s, funding factories, housing and infrastructure.

Internationally, Stresemann pursued a policy of diplomatic engagement. The Locarno Pact of 1925 normalised Germany’s western borders and improved relations with France and Britain. In 1926 Germany joined the League of Nations as a permanent member of the Council — a major rehabilitation of German international standing. The Young Plan of 1929 further reduced reparations. Germany appeared, by the late 1920s, to be a stable democracy integrating into the international community.

The mid-1920s saw a cultural flourishing in Weimar Germany. Berlin became a centre of modern art, cabaret, cinema and experimental theatre. The Bauhaus design school pioneered modernist architecture and craft. Yet this cultural openness was resented by conservative and nationalist Germans who saw it as immoral and un-German. Weimar stability was also more fragile than it appeared: the economy depended on short-term American loans, the political parties rarely cooperated effectively, and extremist parties — both Nazi and Communist — continued to win seats in the Reichstag.

The Depression and the Collapse of Weimar

Stresemann’s death in October 1929 came at the worst possible moment. Weeks later, the Wall Street Crash triggered a global economic depression. American banks recalled their loans to Germany, businesses collapsed and unemployment soared: by early 1932 approximately six million Germans were out of work. The economic catastrophe destroyed the fragile consensus that had sustained Weimar democracy during the recovery years.

Weimar’s proportional representation system produced fragmented parliaments where coalition governments struggled to agree. Between 1930 and 1932 chancellors governed increasingly by emergency decree under Article 48, bypassing the Reichstag. Support for the Nazi Party surged: in the 1928 election the Nazis won under 3% of the vote; by July 1932 they were the largest party with 37.4%. In January 1933, President Hindenburg appointed Hitler as chancellor, believing conservative advisers could control him. That miscalculation ended the Weimar Republic.

lesson_title: Rise and consolidation of Nazi power, 1933-1934
content_html:
Why Did Germans Turn to the Nazis?

By 1932 the Nazi Party had become the largest party in Germany. Several overlapping factors explain this surge. The Great Depression, which began in 1929, had caused approximately six million Germans to lose their jobs by early 1932. Weimar's coalition governments seemed paralysed and ineffective. Traditional parties of the centre and left lost the confidence of voters who blamed them for Germany's humiliation under the Treaty of Versailles and the economic disaster.

The Nazis offered simple, powerful messages: a strong Germany restored to greatness, punishment of the groups they blamed for Germany's troubles (Jews, communists, the Weimar politicians), full employment, and national unity. Their propaganda — mass rallies, striking imagery and the cult of Hitler's personal leadership — was carefully managed. The party also ran effective local organisations that provided welfare in the early Depression years, winning grassroots loyalty. While no single group exclusively supported the Nazis, they drew heavily from the middle class, rural voters, Protestants and the young.

Key Fact

In the July 1932 election the Nazis won 37.4% of votes — their highest ever in a free election. In November 1932 support fell to 33.1%, suggesting their peak support had passed. Hitler was nonetheless appointed chancellor on 30 January 1933.

Hitler as Chancellor, January 1933

President Hindenburg disliked and distrusted Hitler but was persuaded by advisers — notably Franz von Papen — that Hitler could be appointed chancellor and then controlled. Papen believed conservative politicians in the cabinet would act as a check on Hitler. On 30 January 1933 Hindenburg appointed Hitler as chancellor. This proved a catastrophic miscalculation. Within eighteen months Hitler had used a series of legal and semi-legal steps to transform Germany from a democratic republic into a one-party dictatorship.

The Reichstag Fire and the Emergency Decree

On 27 February 1933 the Reichstag building was set on fire. A young Dutch communist named Marinus van der Lubbe was found at the scene and arrested. Hitler immediately claimed the fire was evidence of a communist plot to overthrow the government. The next day Hindenburg signed the Reichstag Fire Decree, suspending civil liberties including freedom of speech, press and assembly, and allowing arrest without trial. Over 4,000 communists were arrested in the following weeks, removing the Nazi Party's main political rivals from the election campaign then under way.

On 23 March 1933, the Reichstag passed the Enabling Act, which gave Hitler the power to make laws without consulting parliament for four years. To pass it required a two-thirds majority. The Nazis had arrested communist deputies and intimidated opposition members. Only the Social Democrats voted against. SA and SS troops lined the chamber. The Enabling Act was the legal foundation of Hitler's dictatorship; from this point, Germany's government operated outside the Weimar Constitution.

Gleichschaltung: Coordinating German Society

Gleichschaltung — literally 'co-ordination' or 'bringing into line' — was the process by which the Nazis extended their control over every institution in Germany during 1933. Trade unions were banned in May 1933 and replaced by the Nazi Labour Front. All political parties other than the NSDAP were banned by July 1933. State governments were stripped of their independence and replaced by Nazi-appointed governors. Newspapers, radio and film came under the control of Joseph Goebbels's new Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda.

The Night of the Long Knives, June 1934

The SA (Sturmabteilung — the Nazi stormtroopers) numbered approximately three million by 1934 and its leader, Ernst Röhm, demanded that the SA absorb the army into a 'people's militia'. This alarmed the regular army, which Hitler needed to rearm Germany and secure his regime. Conservative politicians and business leaders also feared the SA's radical, street-fighting culture. Over the weekend of 29–30 June 1934, Hitler ordered the SS and Gestapo to arrest and execute SA leaders. Röhm was shot in his prison cell.

The purge — known as the Night of the Long Knives — killed approximately 85 to 200 people, including Röhm and other SA leaders, along with conservative opponents like former chancellor Kurt von Schleicher. The purge demonstrated the ruthlessness of the Nazi regime and reassured the army that its position was secure under Hitler.

Key Fact

After President Hindenburg's death on 2 August 1934, Hitler merged the offices of chancellor and president, declaring himself Führer and commander-in-chief. The army swore a personal oath of loyalty to Hitler. Germany was now a full dictatorship.

The Police State

Control was maintained through a network of terror. The SS and Gestapo monitored, arrested and intimidated opponents. The Gestapo relied heavily on denunciations from ordinary citizens — neighbours, colleagues and family members reporting suspected disloyalty. Concentration camps had been established as early as March 1933 at Dachau; by 1934 they held political prisoners — communists, socialists, trade unionists and others deemed enemies of the state. Fear was an effective tool: people self-censored because they did not know who might report them.

By August 1934 Hitler held complete formal power: chancellor, president, supreme commander of the armed forces, and Führer of the Nazi Party. All other parties were banned, the press was controlled, civil liberties suspended. However, in practice the regime still relied on the cooperation of existing institutions — the civil service, the judiciary and the army — many of whose members were not committed Nazis. The consolidation of power was therefore more a dismantling of democratic safeguards than an overnight transformation of every aspect of German life.

lesson_title: Life under the Nazis, 1933-1939
content_html:
The Nazi Economy, 1933–1939

One of the Nazis' most important early successes was tackling unemployment. When Hitler came to power in January 1933, approximately six million Germans were out of work. By 1938 unemployment had fallen to under half a million. How was this achieved? Partly through public works programmes — building the autobahn motorway network — and rearmament, which pumped money into heavy industry. The government also removed women from statistics by encouraging them to leave the workforce, and conscription from 1935 reduced the number of men counted as unemployed.

Finance minister Hjalmar Schacht managed the economy between 1933 and 1937, using a 'New Plan' (1934) to manage imports and exports and 'mefo bills' — government IOUs — to fund rearmament secretly without appearing to breach the Treaty of Versailles. From 1936 Hermann Göring supervised the Four Year Plan, designed to make Germany self-sufficient (autarky) and war-ready within four years. By 1939 Germany had substantially rearmed but had not achieved autarky.

Key Fact

Unemployment fell from approximately 6 million in 1933 to under 500,000 by 1938. However, real wages for workers barely recovered to 1929 levels, and the regime's economic growth depended heavily on rearmament spending — not sustainable peacetime prosperity.

Control of Workers: the DAF

In May 1933 the Nazis banned all independent trade unions and replaced them with the German Labour Front (DAF). Workers could no longer strike or negotiate freely. The 'Strength through Joy' (KdF) programme offered workers subsidised leisure activities — concerts, theatre, sports facilities and holidays — as a means of building loyalty and managing morale without granting genuine economic power. The 'Beauty of Labour' programme improved some factory conditions. In practice, workers gained material benefits but surrendered all collective bargaining rights.

Women in Nazi Germany: The Three Ks

The Nazis had a clearly defined role for women: Kinder, Küche, Kirche — children, kitchen, church. Women were expected to leave paid employment, marry, and bear as many children as possible to grow the German 'racial community'. The regime offered financial incentives: a marriage loan of 1,000 Reichsmarks was offered when women left work, with a quarter written off for each child born. By 1939 the birth rate had risen modestly compared to the early 1930s, though it never reached Nazi targets.

Women were removed from professional positions — female doctors, lawyers and civil servants were pushed out during 1933–1935. However, the ideology was pragmatic: as rearmament created labour shortages, women were gradually drawn back into the workforce from the late 1930s, demonstrating the tension between Nazi ideology and economic reality.

Nazi ideology reshaped the school curriculum. History was rewritten to glorify Germany's past and Hitler's role. Biology taught racial theory — the supposed superiority of the 'Aryan' race and the danger of 'inferior' groups. Physical education expanded, reflecting the Nazi emphasis on military fitness. Jewish teachers were dismissed. Textbooks were replaced with Nazi-approved versions. Teachers were required to join the National Socialist Teachers' League and teach approved content. By 1936 around 97% of teachers had joined the organisation.

The Hitler Youth

Outside school, the Hitler Youth organised boys from 14 to 18, with the Jungvolk for younger boys. Girls aged 14–18 joined the League of German Girls (BDM), focused on fitness and preparation for motherhood. Membership was made compulsory in 1936. Activities included camping, sports, marching and patriotic songs, all designed to build physical fitness and loyalty to Hitler. Many young Germans embraced the movement enthusiastically; others found the discipline oppressive. By 1939 the Hitler Youth had approximately eight million members.

Key Fact

Hitler Youth membership was made compulsory in 1936. By 1939 it had around eight million members. However, some young Germans resisted — the Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth groups rejected Nazi conformity, listening to American music and challenging Hitler Youth authority.

The Treatment of Jews, 1933–1939

Antisemitism was central to Nazi ideology. From 1933 onwards the regime introduced a series of increasingly severe measures targeting Germany's Jewish population, which numbered approximately 500,000 — less than 1% of the German population. Jews were dismissed from civil service jobs under the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service (April 1933). Jewish-owned businesses were boycotted. Jews were excluded from cultural, legal and academic life.

In September 1935, the Nuremberg Laws stripped Jews of German citizenship and banned marriage and sexual relationships between Jews and non-Jews ('racial pollution'). Jews were defined by ancestry — anyone with three or four Jewish grandparents was classified as Jewish. By 1938, approximately 150,000 Jews had emigrated, but many lacked the money or the receiving country's willingness to take them.

On the night of 9–10 November 1938, a wave of violence swept across Germany and Austria. Approximately 7,500 Jewish-owned businesses were destroyed, around 1,400 synagogues were burned, at least 91 Jews were killed, and approximately 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps. The event became known as Kristallnacht — the 'Night of Broken Glass'. Although presented as a spontaneous public reaction to the assassination of a German diplomat, Kristallnacht was organised with Nazi Party involvement. It marked a sharp escalation in the persecution of Jews, foreshadowing the more systematic violence to come.

lesson_title: Life during the Second World War
content_html:
The German Home Front in the Early War Years

Germany went to war in September 1939 with an economy that had not fully converted to a wartime footing. In the early years of the war, as German forces won rapid victories across Europe, the regime tried to shield the German civilian population from significant sacrifice. Consumer goods remained available longer than in other belligerent nations, and rationing — though introduced — was less severe than in Britain during the same period. The regime feared that excessive hardship would undermine popular support, having studied how the Home Front had collapsed in 1918.

Joseph Goebbels managed information carefully, ensuring early German victories were celebrated while setbacks were minimised or explained away. Radio broadcasts, cinema newsreels and newspapers all presented a filtered picture of the war.

Key Fact

After the German defeat at Stalingrad in early 1943, Goebbels declared 'total war' in a speech at the Berlin Sportpalast on 18 February 1943. This meant the full mobilisation of the German economy and society for the war effort — longer working hours, more women in factories, and severe reductions in consumer goods.

Total War: Changing Conditions from 1943

The turning point came with the German surrender at Stalingrad in February 1943. Approximately 300,000 German and Axis soldiers had been encircled; roughly 91,000 surrendered, including Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus. The defeat shattered the myth of German invincibility and marked the beginning of a strategic retreat on the Eastern Front. Goebbels responded by mobilising public sentiment, calling for sacrifice in his 'total war' speech.

From 1943, conditions on the German Home Front deteriorated sharply. Albert Speer, as Armaments Minister, reorganised industrial production to maximise military output. Women were increasingly drafted into factory work despite the earlier ideology that women belonged in the home. Food and goods rationing tightened. By 1944–1945, Allied bombing campaigns — both British night bombing and American daylight precision raids — were causing massive civilian casualties and destroying industrial capacity in German cities.

Allied bombing caused enormous destruction in German cities. The firebombing of Hamburg in July–August 1943 (Operation Gomorrah) killed an estimated 37,000 people and left approximately one million homeless. Dresden was firebombed in February 1945 with heavy civilian casualties, though exact figures remain disputed by historians. The bombing disrupted industrial production, forced the dispersal of factories and consumed massive German anti-aircraft resources — diverting weapons and personnel from the front.

Opposition to the Nazis During the War

Organised opposition to the Nazi regime was extremely dangerous, but it existed. The White Rose was a small student resistance group at Munich University. Hans and Sophie Scholl and their associates distributed leaflets calling for passive resistance against Hitler's regime. They were arrested in February 1943, tried before the People's Court, and executed by guillotine. Their moral courage became a symbol of principled opposition to Nazism.

The most significant act of resistance came from within the military. On 20 July 1944, Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg placed a bomb at Hitler's military headquarters at Rastenburg — the July Plot. Hitler survived because the briefcase containing the bomb was moved behind a heavy table leg. Approximately 5,000 people were arrested in the subsequent purge; around 200 were executed, including Stauffenberg. The plot's failure strengthened Hitler's belief in his destiny and led to even more brutal repression.

Key Fact

The White Rose distributed anti-Nazi leaflets in 1942–43; its leaders, Hans and Sophie Scholl, were executed in February 1943. The July Plot (1944) was a military attempt to assassinate Hitler; it failed and approximately 5,000 were arrested in reprisals.

The Final Solution

The persecution of Jews escalated dramatically once the war began. In territories conquered by Germany — Poland, the Soviet Union and beyond — mobile killing units called Einsatzgruppen shot hundreds of thousands of Jews, Roma, Soviet officials and others in mass killings. The scale of murder by shooting was enormous — at Babi Yar near Kyiv in September 1941, approximately 33,771 Jews were killed over two days.

At the Wannsee Conference on 20 January 1942, senior Nazi officials coordinated the bureaucratic machinery for the systematic murder of all European Jews, a programme they termed the 'Final Solution to the Jewish Question'. Death camps were established at Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno and Majdanek in occupied Poland. These were industrialised killing centres equipped with gas chambers. The majority of victims were murdered in gas chambers using Zyklon B at Auschwitz or carbon monoxide at the other camps. Historians estimate that approximately six million Jewish people were murdered in the Holocaust between 1941 and 1945.

By early 1945 the Soviet Red Army was advancing rapidly from the east and Allied forces from the west. Germany's cities lay in ruins from bombing; millions were displaced. Hitler retreated to a bunker beneath the Berlin Reich Chancellery. On 30 April 1945 he died by suicide as Soviet forces entered the city. Germany surrendered unconditionally on 8 May 1945 — known as VE Day (Victory in Europe Day). The war had killed an estimated 5–7 million German civilians and soldiers.
